title: Sponsor-a-Lifeline Satellite Messaging for Missionaries
angle: Pairing 2: Space economy x Weird/niche/overlooked markets (hobbies, collectibles, faith, subcultures)
one_liner: A church-sponsored satellite messaging line plus supporter-update relay for missionaries, Bible translators and mission-aviation crews in no-coverage areas, sold to mission agencies as duty of care.
customer: Mission agencies with 50-2,000 field workers and the sending churches that sponsor individual workers.
problem: Field workers live outside coverage and agencies carry duty of care using a patchwork of individual satellite communicators. Missionaries also fund themselves through supporter updates, which stall when connectivity is bad. Churches want a tangible way to care for their people, yet direct-to-cell carriers still do not know how to price or differentiate satellite service.
solution: A neutral bundle: direct-to-cell or handheld messaging across whichever networks work (Iridium NTN, Starlink direct-to-cell, others) plus an agency dashboard with check-in cadence, geofenced security alerts and evacuation triggers. Short satellite texts are compiled into a 'prayer letter' for supporters, and a sponsor page (for example 'Sponsor Anna's lifeline at $18 per month') keeps privacy controls.
why_now: Satellite-to-phone partnerships are multiplying but 'key questions remain unresolved' on pricing and value (Satellite Today, Sept 2026). Iridium NTN Direct is expected later in 2026, and Starlink ARPU falling from $81 to $66 signals cheaper plans. Carriers and resellers need verticals with a willing payer.
revenue_model: $15-25 per field worker per month paid by the agency or sponsors, a $150-200 hardware and setup margin, and enterprise duty-of-care dashboard tiers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the sending church or agency, not the traveler, and the value of connectivity is fundraising continuity as much as SOS. A 'sponsor a lifeline' framing turns safety hardware into recurring giving.
first_30_days: Approach 5 small and mid-sized agencies through a mission-agency association. Offer 20-seat pilots at $150 setup plus $18 per month per seat. Write prayer-letter templates and test the sponsor page with two sending churches.

title: Night Shift Tox Bulletin for Opioid Settlement Counties
one_liner: A no-patient-data network where rural ER nurses text in what they are seeing, turned into weekly local drug-supply alerts sold to counties spending opioid settlement money.
customer: County opioid settlement councils and public health departments, EMS medical directors, jails, harm-reduction programs and rural hospitals. Paid by county contract from opioid settlement funds.
problem: New adulterants show up in a rural ER as a pattern before they show up in any dataset. Examples are patients who are sedated but not responding to naloxone, or patients with a slow heart rate and low blood pressure that is not the usual opioid picture, or brutal withdrawal with high blood pressure. Confirmatory lab results take weeks or months. Surveillance networks are concentrated in academic and urban centers, so a rural county may learn about something two states over long after the ER has seen it. Nurses talk to each other in the break room and on private Facebook groups, but they have no safe way to alert the county, EMS, jail or harm-reduction workers. Hospital administrations do not want a nurse speaking for the hospital.
solution: A 30-second SMS or Signal report with no patient identifiers: date, county, number of patients, presentation flags, response to reversal, what the patients said they took, and any new physical findings such as wounds. Reports are aggregated with a minimum threshold (for example 3 or more per week) to protect privacy. The service returns a plain-language weekly county bulletin to nurses, EMS, jail medical staff and harm-reduction groups, and triggers targeted drug-checking or lab testing of residue with a lab partner. Include a jail-specific alert because withdrawal from newer sedatives is dangerous inside a jail.
why_now: Medetomidine, a veterinary sedative, is now in the illicit supply well beyond Philadelphia. Wastewater data showed it in at least one of 14 states every week from October 2025 to January 2026, and California published an emerging issue brief in April 2026. The main ER sentinel program has only about 17 to 20 academic centers, so rural emergency departments are barely covered. Tens of billions of dollars in opioid settlement funds are arriving in local hands, and county councils are actively looking for evidence-based data and surveillance projects.
revenue_model: $12-36k per year per county or multi-county region, with a lower price for small counties and bundled state contracts through state opioid settlement offices. A secondary product is a per-test fee when the network triggers drug-checking or lab confirmation, and a jail early-warning subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not lab capacity. It is a trusted channel for the person who sees it first and has no authority to speak. A night-shift nurse is a better early-warning sensor than a dashboard, and the data is qualitative and deliberately human: 'this doesn't look like what we normally see.' Because you can build it with no PHI, nurses can contribute from their own phones off shift without touching hospital systems. Other tools (ODMAP, poison center feeds) are built for incident counts and law enforcement or EMS reports, not clinical pattern recognition.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 rural ER and night nurses from state nurses' groups and private Facebook communities. Send a free weekly bulletin to three neighboring counties and their EMS agencies. Attend an opioid settlement council meeting (agendas and minutes are public) in one of them. Offer a paid six-month pilot at $1,000 per month. Line up one lab partner for confirmatory testing. Get a lawyer to review the no-PHI reporting language and publish a clear policy telling nurses to leave out anything identifiable.

title: Rural Jail Pharmacy-in-a-Box for Independents
one_liner: Turn the local independent's blister packing, delivery and controlled-substance discipline into a per-inmate contract for the county jail that the sheriff is afraid of.
customer: Sheriffs, jail administrators and county commissions running jails of about 20-150 beds, whose risk pools and insurers care about medication liability. Independent pharmacies are a second customer, licensing the playbook and software.
problem: Jail medication is a sheriff's biggest lawsuit exposure: missed doses, withdrawal, wrong-inmate errors, controlled-substance counts. Small jails run it with a deputy, a clipboard and a nurse who visits two days a week. Mail-order jail pharmacies take 3-5 days, so first-night meds come from the ER or a deputy's personal trip to the drugstore. Buprenorphine and other opioid-treatment mandates funded by opioid settlements add complexity. Meanwhile local independents already run the identical workflow for nursing homes.
solution: A repeatable program with same-day intake verification (call the outside pharmacy, check the PDMP). Barcode blister-packed med pass with an offline-capable eMAR on a tablet. Controlled-substance counts with dual sign-off and photo audit. An emergency kit and a monthly consultant-pharmacist review. A 30-day bridge supply at release. Sold as a playbook, software and group-purchasing bundle so any independent can become the county's jail pharmacy, with master agreements through state association-of-counties risk pools.
why_now: Wellpath's late-2024 bankruptcy and the contract turnover that followed left counties scrambling for medical vendors. Deaths-in-custody litigation keeps rising. Opioid-settlement dollars are flowing to county jails for medication for opioid use disorder. A growing number of state Medicaid reentry waivers require medication continuity at release. Independents need any revenue line that does not depend on PBM reimbursement.
revenue_model: County per-diem or monthly retainer (roughly $1,500-6,000 a month per small jail, to be validated by state). The pharmacy pays a 10-15% platform fee plus $300-600 a month for the software. Additional revenue from risk-pool partnership programs and discharge-supply services.
non_obvious_insight: Rural jail medication is not a healthcare problem, it is a liability problem the sheriff cannot outsource to a national vendor that ships in five days. The real buyer is the county risk pool and insurer, and the independent pharmacist next door is the only entity that can deliver in thirty minutes. Small contracts often fall below county bid thresholds, and the sheriff already knows the pharmacist by first name.
first_30_days: The pharmacist calls the sheriff in their own county and offers a 60-day pilot at cost. Audit the jail's med room and write a one-page deficiency list. Propose eMAR plus packaging. Check the state pharmacy board's rules for institutional or correctional pharmacy licensure. Pitch the results to the state sheriffs' association and the county risk pool, and recruit two neighboring independents to copy the model.

title: Risk and Insurance Stack for Pickleball Venues
one_liner: Incident logging, e-waivers, court-safety audits and an insurance program that make independent racquet venues insurable at fair prices.
customer: Independent indoor and outdoor pickleball and padel venue operators, plus HOAs and municipal recreation departments.
problem: Indoor pickleball operators report difficulty finding coverage, typical policies carry $1-5M general liability, injuries rose about 6.8x between 2017 and 2022, and noise disputes now end in lawsuits. Insurers lack venue-level data, so they price the category rather than the operator.
solution: Step one: $149-299 per month software with e-waivers, incident reporting, a photo-evidence court, lighting and fencing audit checklist and staff training. Step two: use the aggregated data to place operators with specialty carriers as a broker or MGA and negotiate premium credits for documented venues.
why_now: Venue counts have boomed while commentators now say the boom is starting to crack, which makes insurers and lenders demand evidence; no standard exists.
revenue_model: SaaS $149-299 per venue per month plus 10-15 percent broker or MGA commission on premiums of $8-30k per policy.
non_obvious_insight: Data is the product: when insurers lack venue-level evidence they price to the average, so the operator who documents beats the average. Start as software, then capture the insurance economics.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed broker, audit 10 venues in one metro, produce an insurer-ready risk dossier for each, and take 20 dossiers to two specialty carriers.

title: Backyard Telescopes as Cubesat Finders
angle: Pairing 2: Space economy x Weird/niche/overlooked markets (hobbies, collectibles, faith, subcultures)
one_liner: Pay owners of consumer smart telescopes to image newly deployed smallsats, so operators learn which object is theirs and whether their panels deployed.
customer: University teams, startups and small operators flying on rideshare missions with 100+ payloads, plus satellite insurers and brokers who want an independent health signal.
problem: After rideshare deployments the public catalog lags days to weeks and objects are mis-associated. A silent satellite may be dead or merely misidentified, and operators without their own ground networks burn weeks of contact attempts. 2025 saw 321 orbital launches and 4,517 satellites deployed, so far more unfunded small operators face this.
solution: A client for popular smart telescopes (Seestar and Unistellar class) receives tasking for predicted twilight passes and uploads wide-field frames. The server solves streak astrometry and photometry, returning position updates to improve the operator's orbit, an ID confirmation, and tumble rate and brightness changes that hint at panel or antenna deployment. Owners are paid credits per validated pass, with leaderboards.
why_now: Rideshare cadence and cheap launch flood the catalog with small, poorly funded payloads. Thousands of app-controlled smart telescopes now sit in backyards, AI streak detection is cheap, and the brief flags rising conjunction-screening load for operators.
revenue_model: $1,500-4,000 per mission for a LEOP identification and deployment package, plus a $500 per month monitoring subscription. About a third of revenue goes to observer payouts, and insurers pay per-object fees.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a fast, independent 'is it alive and deployed?' second opinion, not images. Space-situational-awareness firms build expensive sensor networks, whereas hobbyists supply sensors that are paid for in status and gear credits, at a fraction of the cost.
first_30_days: Use open-source astrometry and streak tools. Recruit 150 smart-telescope owners in maker forums and Discords. Take the public payload list of the next rideshare mission, cold-email 3 small operators with a free pilot, and convert two to paid at $1,500 on the following mission.

title: Rolling Bio-Uplift Trials for Frontier Labs
one_liner: A standing cohort of novices and benign-proxy wet-lab tasks that measures whether each new AI model actually helps people do biology, within weeks of release.
customer: Frontier AI lab safeguards and preparedness teams, government AI safety institutes, and operators of bio-AI verification programs; insurers later.
problem: The main large RCT (Active Site, n=153, run June-August 2025, published February 2026) found workflow completion of 5.2% with LLMs versus 6.6% with the internet. Task uplift was 1.42x and non-significant. Forecasters had predicted 27% uplift against 5% actual. By publication the tested models were about a year old. Labs now grant relaxed safeguards to verified users (Anthropic's Sept 17 program) without current evidence on which wet-lab tasks models actually change.
solution: Maintain a trained standing cohort of 100-200 novices with baselined tacit skill, in a BSL-1 lab with IRB approval done once. Use pre-approved benign-proxy tasks (plasmid construction with harmless markers, protein purification, cell culture, plaque assay with a harmless phage). Randomize model access versus internet access and return results within 2-3 weeks of each model checkpoint.
why_now: The RCT showed tacit bench skill, not knowledge, is the bottleneck, and it also exposed evaluation lag. Frontier labs ship models every few months. New verification programs make evidence on actual uplift commercially valuable to both labs and legitimate users.
revenue_model: $150-400k per model evaluation, $600k-1.5M annual retainers, and calibrated benchmark licenses to verification-program operators.
non_obvious_insight: The frontier is mostly measured with text quizzes, while risk (and benefit to legitimate labs) lives in hands-on tacit skill. Speed and cadence, not a one-off academic RCT, is the product. Active Site is a nonprofit incumbent, so expect to partner or license protocols. The cohort and lab double as a training and vetting pipeline for a bench network.
first_30_days: Contact Active Site and METR alumni for protocol and IRB templates and explore licensing rather than duplicating. Secure BSL-1 space. Recruit 40 novices and run a 3-week pilot on two open-weight models to publish methodology. Pitch 3 safeguards teams and 2 government safety bodies on a $100k pilot.

title: GLP-1 Menu Labeling Layer for Independent Restaurants
one_liner: A cheap per-dish protein, fiber and portion labeling and half-portion pricing tool that tells the 12% of diners on GLP-1 drugs which dishes fit, published wherever they look.
customer: Owner-operated independent restaurants and small groups (2-30 locations), plus campus and hospital cafeterias, that sell through delivery apps and Google Maps. They pay $199 setup and $39/month.
problem: About 11-12% of US adults now take GLP-1 drugs, up from 3% in 2024 (KFF poll). Chains have reacted with lighter-portion sections, protein menus and dedicated GLP-1 menus (Olive Garden, Shake Shack, Chipotle, Subway, Smoothie King). Independents have no dietitian, no nutrition data and no way to show which dishes fit. Their menus say nothing about protein grams or half sizes, and independents are exempt from chain menu-labeling rules.
solution: The owner uploads a menu PDF or photo. The tool estimates per-dish calories, protein and fiber as a range, using LLM recipe parsing plus USDA FoodData Central. It tags dishes 'protein-first' or 'light plate' using explicit, published thresholds. It suggests a half-portion or 'box half before it reaches the table' price point that keeps margin (food cost is typically about 30% of price, so a half portion at 65-70% of price holds gross profit). It then auto-publishes to the Google Business Profile menu, DoorDash and Uber Eats descriptions, a QR menu and printable table tents, with a short staff script. All output is worded as an estimate with no medical claims.
why_now: Health-topic search data shows GLP1 at 1.5M monthly searches (+1,011%) and Fibremaxxing +7,900%, and Google's Summergeist report shows fibermaxxing at an all-time high. Chains are now marketing to this group in 2026, so independents are losing a segment that dines out often.
revenue_model: $199 setup, $39/month per location for menu updates, delivery-app syncing and 'reorder tag' analytics. Add-ons: $99 printed table tents and $149 chef-recipe reformulation consult. Later: bundle through POS resellers, delivery-marketing agencies and restaurant associations.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is communication, not the menu. A 2026 survey cited by ABC News found 89% of GLP-1 users wish restaurants 'communicated better about options that promote health and wellness' while 90% say restaurants typically do offer healthy items. The same coverage cites a National Restaurant Association survey that GLP-1 users make 7.6 restaurant purchases a week versus 5.1 for non-users. They want 'half-sized and lunch-sized portions, protein-first options... the ability to box food before it reaches the table' (https://abcnews.com/US/weight-loss-drug-usage-grows-restaurants-offer-glp/story?id=135711648). So the cheapest fix is labeling and relabeling what a kitchen already makes, not building new dishes, and nutrition-lab analysis is unnecessary. Chain moves are documented at https://www.foodingredientsfirst.com/news/glp-1-friendly-menus-food-dining-2026.html and https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/smaller-portions-protein-glp-1s-are-quietly-changing-chain-restaurant-rcna254178, which both say nothing about independents, so that segment is unserved. Search demand: https://explodingtopics.com/health-topics.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the menu parser, estimates and tag thresholds, and have a registered dietitian review the method and disclaimers. Days 8-20: walk into 30 independent restaurants in one dense neighborhood with a free 'GLP-1 menu scorecard' on their own menu, and pitch via the local restaurant association and Toast/Square consultants. Days 21-30: onboard 8-10 paying restaurants, publish updated Google Business Profile and delivery listings, and track half-portion attach rate and new-visitor searches for a case study.

title: Stablecoin Cash-Out Float for Corner Shops
one_liner: Stablecoins made sending money nearly free, so the scarce thing is cash at the last mile, and the margin goes to whoever finances the agents.
customer: Pharmacies, tiendas and kiosks that act as cash-out agents in Colombia, Mexico, Argentina and Nigeria, plus the stablecoin remittance and wallet apps that need them.
problem: A $200 US-to-Colombia transfer costs $12.13 on legacy rails versus about $0.01 in stablecoins, but recipients still want local cash. Small agents run out of float and refuse large withdrawals.
solution: A float-management app that shows each agent's cash position, advances intraday float against next-day USDC settlement and routes recipients to agents with liquidity. The wedge is 100 pharmacies on one remittance corridor for a single anchor partner.
why_now: Nigeria opened a stablecoin sandbox (Aug 12) and Kenya passed digital-currency legislation (Aug 6). Yellow Card is hiring in LatAm and SEA, and Felix has processed $8B over WhatsApp.
revenue_model: A 1-1.5% spread on float turnover plus a per-payout fee from the remitter.
non_obvious_insight: As stablecoin transfer fees go to zero, the margin migrates to the last ten metres of physical cash. This is cash logistics dressed up as fintech.
first_30_days: Sign one wallet or remittance partner as anchor and raise a roughly $50k float line from a debt fund. Onboard 20 pharmacies in one city.

title: Organized Play in a Box for New Card Games
one_liner: A managed service that gives new and crowdfunded trading card games tournament software, judge training, local-game-store onboarding and prize logistics.
customer: New TCG publishers with funded campaigns (for example the Cyberpunk TCG, which raised $28.35M on Kickstarter in April 2026), and their distributors.
problem: Pokemon has sold 85B+ cards, and new TCGs live or die by weekly events at local game stores. First-time creators have big print-run budgets but no rules-aware tournament engine, judge program, store network or prize support. Kickstarter success does not equal retention.
solution: Rules-aware tournament software (decklist validation, banlist updates, Swiss pairing), a certified judge program, store onboarding kits (demo decks, promos, shipping), an event calendar and reporting, and results-integrity tooling.
why_now: The TCG boom and $28M crowdfunding raises create a wave of well-funded first-time publishers. Stores will only stock games with events.
revenue_model: $5-25k per month retainer per game plus $10-30 per event and margin on store kits.
non_obvious_insight: Kickstarter funds the print run, but retention is in weekly events, and store owners only back games that have them. The infrastructure is game-agnostic, so it amortizes across many small TCGs.
first_30_days: Pitch 20 creators of funded TCG campaigns above $250k. Run a pilot kit at 20 stores. Assemble an open-source tournament engine and sell the first two retainers.

title: Muthoot-Style Gold Loans for America's Junk Drawers
one_liner: A mail-in, XRF-assayed loan against gold and jewelry at roughly 24-36% APR, versus 200%-plus at a typical US pawn shop, run through licensed pawn partners for people who need $300-$5,000 and have idle gold worth far more with gold trading around $4,100-$4,500 an ounce.
customer: Middle-income households aged 35-65 with jewelry and coins in a drawer and thin or damaged credit who need a few hundred to a few thousand dollars for a car repair, rent gap or tax bill. Small-business owners with a cash-flow gap are the second segment.
problem: Cash-for-gold buyers pay a fraction of melt value with no way to get the piece back. Pawn shops charge 10-25% a month. Payday and title lenders charge triple-digit APRs. The only cheap collateral-backed product is stigmatized, store-based and priced for rent rather than risk, so many people with real assets choose worse options or sell irreplaceable pieces at a loss.
solution: Mail an insured kit (or drop off at a partner pawn store). On receipt, run an XRF assay and weigh, then offer 70-75% of melt value within hours and pay by ACH. Redeem by paying principal plus interest, and the piece comes back insured. If the borrower does not repay, the gold is sold at melt with any surplus returned where state law requires. There is no collections calling and no credit reporting. Interest is about 2% a month falling for repeat borrowers. Hedge the collateral pool with gold futures. Launch through a licensed pawnbroker as lender of record, then license state by state.
why_now: Gold has traded roughly between $4,100 and $4,500 an ounce in September 2026, so a drawer of old 14k jewelry is worth several times what it was in 2022. Indian gold-loan lenders (Muthoot, Rupeek and others) have shown that 9-25% APR gold lending is profitable at scale, while US pawn remains a fragmented, store-based, high-rate market. Cheap XRF analyzers, insured shipping and instant ACH remove the storefront cost that justified those US rates.
revenue_model: Interest of 1.5-2.5% a month on outstanding loans, plus a small handling fee on loans under $500, plus surplus on forfeited gold sold above the loan amount. Funded by a private-credit warehouse line at low double-digit cost of capital. Because loans are 70-75% of a liquid commodity's melt value, credit losses are close to hedging and shipping costs.
non_obvious_insight: The 200%-plus APR of US pawn is not a price for risk, because collateral makes the loss very small. It is a price for store rent, low volume and stigma. Remove the storefront and the mass-market stigma (customers are gold owners with poor liquidity, not desperate borrowers) and you can undercut incumbents 5-8x on price and still earn better returns on capital than a bank.
first_30_days: Sign a licensed pawnbroker in Texas or Florida as lender of record so you inherit their license and compliance, including police reporting of transactions. Buy an XRF analyzer and a rated insured vault or use a custody partner. Raise about $250k to fund the first 50-100 loans. Buy search and social ads that intercept 'sell my gold' intent and publish the true APR up front. First loans should close within 4-6 weeks, and the pilot's default and hedging data becomes the pitch for a credit line.

title: Contingency-Fee Meter Audits for Water Utilities
one_liner: Test the big commercial and industrial meters that under-register, replace them, and take a share of the new billed revenue for two years.
customer: Mid-size water and wastewater utilities (20k-500k connections) with large commercial bases, private regulated water companies, and utilities serving new large loads such as data centers and fabs. The utility pays from recovered revenue.
problem: Everyone sells AI leak detection, but in many audits apparent losses (meter under-registration, billing errors, unauthorized use) are comparable to real losses. Large compound meters under-register at low flow, and 1% of a data center's consumption is a lot of money. Utilities under rate pressure and drought-reduced volumes have no capex budget for meter programs.
solution: Prioritize the top 5% of accounts using billing anomalies (size versus consumption history). Field-test meters with a mobile test bench and clamp-on verification, then repair or replace. The company fronts the work and takes 20-35% of incremental revenue for 24 months. Software ranks accounts, and reports feed the AWWA-style utility audit.
why_now: Drought cuts volumes and rate pressure is intense. Private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 and must justify revenue. New industrial loads make each meter worth more.
revenue_model: 20-35% of incremental billed revenue for two years, with no upfront cost to the utility.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders chase leaks, which need capital and crews. Meter recovery is immediate cash with no capex approval, so it is easy to say yes to. Private and special-district utilities can sign contingency deals without a full municipal procurement.
first_30_days: Target three investor-owned utilities and two special districts. Offer a free desktop analysis of their top 200 commercial accounts using billing data. Test the ten most suspicious meters as a proof-of-value, and sign a contingency contract on the results.

title: Bale Grade Audits With Premium Sharing
one_liner: Independent PET and HDPE bale audits, plus MRF line tuning paid from the price uplift, to turn 'commodity bales' into measured, spec-priced material.
customer: Independent MRFs selling plastic bales (pay a share of uplift) and the surviving US reclaimers, who pay for supplier scoring and dispute referee services.
problem: Feedstock PET bales hit 1.44 cents/lb in April 2026 and seven of about 30 US reclaimers closed. Yet New Jersey delayed its food-contact PCR mandate citing constrained food-grade supply, while recyclers say HDPE blow-mold supply is 'not constrained.' That points to a quality-tier mismatch, not a shortage.
solution: Third-party bale audits (manual composition sort, handheld NIR, moisture and weight) that produce a bale spec sheet. A tuning playbook for optical-sorter recipes and QC pickers. Contracts that pay MRFs on measured tier and give reclaimers a lot-level dispute referee.
why_now: The 2026 price collapse and reclaimer closures leave the remaining buyers desperate for predictable quality. The mandate delays mean brands cannot lock supply, so spec-priced material becomes the negotiating currency.
revenue_model: $150-400 per audited load, plus 25-35% of documented price uplift for 6-12 months, plus an annual supplier-scoring subscription for reclaimers.
non_obvious_insight: The 'shortage' insiders cite is a shortage of known-quality material. A measured bale is a different commodity, and no third party captures the gap between 1.44 cents and reclaimer-grade pricing because no one measures it.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 independent MRFs and 1 reclaimer. Manually audit 30 bales and publish the anonymized quality spread. Offer a 6-month uplift-share deal. Buy or borrow a handheld NIR ($10-25K) and standardize the photo protocol.

title: Keep the 58-Year-Old Machinist Two Years Longer
one_liner: Carrier-co-funded ergonomic and assistive-tech programs that delay retirements instead of chasing new hires.
customer: Manufacturers with 30-300 employees and an older workforce. Workers' comp carriers and brokers co-fund it through loss-control budgets and premium credits.
problem: The industry chases Deloitte and Manufacturing Institute's 3.8M hires needed by 2033, with 1.9M possibly unfilled. Their 2024 report stresses retention, not just applicants. About 60% of manufacturing firms have owners aged 55+. Each retiring senior machinist takes years of tacit skill, and recruiting and training replacements is slow and costly.
solution: A 90-day Longevity Program. It starts with an ergonomic assessment of every role held by workers aged 50+. Then it installs a kit of lift assists, tilting fixtures, better lighting and vibration-damped tool holders, plus optional exoskeleton pilots for overhead work. It also designs phased-retirement roles (for example, mentor three days a week). It tracks injuries and retention against a baseline.
why_now: Manufacturing jobs are up 58k since the December 2025 low, so labor is tightening. Announced reshoring hires land 12-24 months after announcements. Lift-assist and exoskeleton hardware is now cheap enough for small shops.
revenue_model: $8-25k per program plus about $150 per employee per month for monitoring and a training-video library. Finder fees from carriers. Optional performance pricing tied to retention.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest hire is the one who does not retire. Insurers already fund loss control for exactly this age group, so the shop's cost is partly paid by a third party with a matching incentive. My rough estimate is that one avoided senior-machinist retirement is worth well over $100k in replacement, scrap and customer risk.
first_30_days: Call loss-control reps at three regional workers' comp carriers or brokers. Offer three free shop assessments. Document before-and-after injury and absence data. Use the results to sell paid programs to the shops.

title: Parametric Insurance on Colorado River Shortage
one_liner: Insurance and hedges that pay out when official Colorado River operating triggers or reservoir projections cross agreed thresholds, sold to large industrial and municipal water buyers.
customer: Chip fabs, data centers, breweries, resorts, master-planned developers and municipal utilities that depend on Lower Basin supplies. Buyers pay premiums, and reinsurance and capital-markets funds take the risk.
problem: Powell plus Mead storage is about 36% and 95% of the basin is in drought. About $1.4T of annual activity is exposed, yet businesses cannot hedge water-supply or rate shocks except by capex. Until this year the rules were too ambiguous to write a contract against.
solution: Start with a Lower Basin water-supply risk index and term sheets, sold to muni-bond investors and industrial water buyers. Then build a parametric product that pays on published operating triggers or reservoir projections, funded through a surplus-lines or Lloyd's partner with an experienced weather-risk insurer. Payouts fund contingency supply, recycling or trucked water.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Record of Decision set the 2027-2036 operating framework, converting political ambiguity into published rules that a contract can reference. Capital-markets investors seek risks uncorrelated with catastrophe.
revenue_model: Premium (a percentage of limit), analytics licensing before any policy is issued, and a share of fund fees.
non_obvious_insight: The ROD makes the river's rules legible, which is the precondition for a derivative. The correlated hydrology scares traditional insurers, but that is exactly what non-catastrophe capital wants to hold.
first_30_days: Build the risk index from Reclamation's public 24-Month Study projections and reservoir data. Interview 10 fab, data-center and utility water managers on what loss they fear. Approach one weather-risk reinsurer and one ILS fund. First revenue comes from analytics sold to bond funds and industrial users.

title: One Guide, Twelve Languages: Live-Dubbed Tours
one_liner: The guide speaks once and each guest hears their own language in low-latency synthesised audio, so mixed-language groups share one guide and cities see fewer, fuller groups.
customer: Independent guides, small tour operators and shore-excursion companies in cities that cap groups (Venice, Rome, Florence, Amsterdam, Kyoto), plus guide associations and municipalities.
problem: Language-siloed tours multiply the number of groups on the same street, and group-size caps and guide quotas bind. Guides cannot fill rare-language tours, and whisper systems only amplify the guide's voice.
solution: Guide microphone to live speech translation to each guest's phone, joined by QR with no app install, with per-listener language choice, a glossary of place names, an offline fallback, headcount tools and translated questions back to the guide. Sell a clip mic and hub kit plus per-tour credits.
why_now: Real-time speech-to-speech translation became good enough in 2025 (consumer earbuds now offer live translation and APIs offer realtime speech), eSIM and 5G make connectivity easy, and cities are tightening group caps.
revenue_model: USD 39-99 per guide per month or USD 1-2 per guest, USD 150 kits and municipal licences.
non_obvious_insight: Language silos are a hidden multiplier of overtourism. Merging groups cuts the number of groups without cutting visitors, so guides earn more and cities become allies and customers.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 guides in Rome and Florence, pilot two-language tours then four, and measure latency and guest satisfaction. Approach the guide association with the pilot results.

title: Death Certificate Sign-Off Copilot for Hospices
one_liner: Get physicians to complete valid cause-of-death certifications in hours instead of days, sold to the hospices and care groups that get blamed for the delay, with funeral homes as the free wedge.
customer: Hospice organizations and nursing-home or assisted-living groups. The buyer is the VP of operations or hospice medical director, motivated by family-experience scores and clinician time. Funeral homes use a free version that seeds the data.
problem: Nothing moves until a physician completes the medical section of the death certificate in the state's electronic system. Cremation authorization, burial permits and certified copies for the family all wait. Doctors forget logins, delegate poorly, or enter invalid cause-of-death chains such as 'cardiac arrest', which triggers rejections or medical examiner referrals. A funeral director spends hours per case chasing certifiers, families see the delay as the funeral home's fault, and the cooler fills up while everyone waits.
solution: Phase one is a free web and text tool for funeral homes. They log each pending certificate, and the tool sends the certifier a one-tap reminder with clear instructions and shows a status page. Phase two is the paid hospice product: from the discharge summary or chart export, an AI drafts the Part I/Part II cause-of-death chain in line with NCHS conventions, flags ME-reportable triggers before submission, and routes a mobile magic-link for physician review. In states that allow certifier designees, hospice staff do the data entry. A dashboard shows time-to-certify by physician and site, with escalation rules.
why_now: Electronic death registration systems are now near-universal, so a digital workflow is possible. LLMs can reliably summarize a chart for physician review in a way that wasn't safe or cheap a few years ago. Hospice growth and public CAHPS Hospice scores raise the stakes of family experience. Medical director workloads are rising with physician shortages.
revenue_model: $35-$60 per certificate processed, or $200-$500/month per hospice site plus per-certifier seats. Optional $99/month funeral-home tier with analytics and multi-hospice benchmarking. Later, sell the anonymized time-to-certify benchmark to hospice chains and payers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone blames the funeral home for slowness, but we spend more time chasing doctors than doing the actual work. This 'post-death workflow orphan' sits after the patient leaves the EHR workflow, so no health-tech vendor sees it. The funeral home is the only party who measures days-from-death-to-certificate. So sell backwards: give funeral homes a free chase tool, collect the scorecard on which hospices and doctors are slow, then walk into those hospices with their own numbers.
first_30_days: Build the no-PHI funeral-home chase tool (case ID, certifier name and phone, state) in two weeks. Recruit 15 funeral homes in two states through the state association. After 60 days publish an anonymized 'days-to-certify by hospice' scorecard. Book meetings with the three slowest hospices and offer a $2,000/month pilot with a signed BAA. Have a physician advisor review the cause-of-death logic.

title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.

title: Water Due Diligence for Senior Housing Deals
angle: Pairing 1: Aging/eldercare/silver economy x Water scarcity/infrastructure
one_liner: A 'Phase I for water' that grades a senior living property or CCRC bond on supply security, drought exposure, contamination compliance and in-building Legionella risk before lenders and buyers commit.
customer: HUD-232 and bridge lenders, senior-housing acquirers and Sunbelt developers, CCRC bond underwriters and muni credit analysts, and insurers. Pricing is $4-12k per deal report and $25-60k a year for portfolio subscriptions.
problem: Senior housing occupancy is 90.1%, the highest since 2007, and construction is the lowest since 2012 with a roughly $275B shortfall. New development will restart in Sunbelt states where Colorado River cuts (2027+), groundwater rules, PFAS and lead compliance, and drought restrictions bite. The asset class is uniquely exposed: 24/7 occupancy, heavy laundry, kitchens and cooling towers, frail residents you cannot evacuate, and Legionella that kills mostly older adults. CCRC bonds promise care for life on 30-year horizons, yet a standard environmental Phase I says nothing about water security.
solution: A standard report covering legally deliverable supply, the provider's source portfolio (river, groundwater, reuse), moratorium and curtailment history, a five-year rate outlook, PFAS, lead and nitrate compliance of the serving utility, and an in-building water-management-plan audit (Legionella per CMS and ASHRAE 188, cooling towers). It also covers drought-restriction impacts on operations and NOI sensitivity to a 30% water-cost spike. Output is a letter grade plus capex and insurance recommendations, with a portfolio dashboard for bond analysts.
why_now: Record occupancy and accelerating investment mean a wave of acquisitions and new starts is coming. The Colorado River decision framework landed in Aug 2026, PFAS monitoring starts in 2027, and Texas's data-center water crackdown showed water is now an explicit siting factor.
revenue_model: Per-report fees of $4-12k, annual subscriptions of $25-60k for bond funds and lender credit desks, and remediation referral fees from the sensor and water-treatment vendors that fix the flagged items.
non_obvious_insight: For senior housing, water risk is life-safety, not just cost. Residents cannot leave and the pathogens are lethal, so it should be underwritten like fire risk, yet nobody sells the underwriting standard. The first credible grade becomes the lender checklist item.
first_30_days: Publish a free water-risk map of the 60 largest CCRC and senior-housing bond issuers in Colorado River, Texas and Florida stress zones. Email it to 30 muni analysts and 10 HUD lenders, and offer three discounted deal reports at $3k.

title: Foreign-Ties Clearance Pack for SBIR Startups
one_liner: A fixed-price, agency-ready foreign-involvement and cyber-readiness dossier priced to fit inside the SBIR technical-assistance allowance, so the startup pays nothing out of pocket.
customer: SBIR/STTR Phase I and Phase II applicants and awardees (DoD, DOE, NSF, NIH, EPA). Secondary buyers are seed and VC funds with SBIR-heavy portfolios that need LP-level attestations for their companies.
problem: The Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (S. 3971, signed April 13, 2026, extends SBIR/STTR through FY2031) makes agencies run risk-based due diligence on every applicant. The review covers foreign ownership and financial ties, foreign affiliations of key personnel, licensing deals and joint ventures, and links to the UFLPA, Chinese Military-Industrial Complex, Commerce Entity and Section 889 lists. It also covers cybersecurity practices, patent analysis and employee analysis. Applicants must file disclosures. A 4-person startup has no idea what an agency will find in its cap table (LPs behind the VC funds), co-inventors, or contractors. Agencies may notify of a denial only 'as appropriate', so a rejection may come with no explanation.
solution: A software-plus-analyst service that ingests the cap table, team list, patents and vendor list. It does look-through on investors (SEC Form ADV and Form D, GLEIF, OpenCorporates). It screens every name against the free BIS Consolidated Screening List and the UFLPA and CMIC lists. It checks co-inventor and employee affiliations (USPTO PatentsView, ORCID) and takes a NIST 800-171/SPRS cyber baseline. Output is a disclosure-ready packet, a red-flag remediation memo (for example 'restructure this side letter'), and a yearly re-screen. Sold as a vendor the awardee can pick for technical and business assistance (T&BA) money.
why_now: S. 3971 was signed April 13, 2026. The T&BA allowance was raised to $6,500 per Phase I and $50,000 per Phase II, and it now explicitly covers 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement'. The lapse from October 2025 to April 2026 created a backlog: DOE alone opened about $147M of FY25 Phase II on July 22, 2026, and the FY26 Genesis Mission Phase I is open. Every awardee now faces the new diligence for the first time.
revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,500 flat per Phase I (fits under the $6,500 T&BA cap, so it is free to the founder). $15k to $50k per Phase II package. $1,200 per year for a re-screen subscription when the cap table changes. VC portfolio bundles at $500 to $1,000 per company.
non_obvious_insight: Congress created an earmarked wallet for exactly this service, and the buyer has zero price sensitivity because the money can't be spent on anything else. S. 3971 Section 7 amends Section 9(q) to allow T&BA funds for 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement', up to $6,500 (Phase I) and $50,000 (Phase II) per project, and lets recipients choose their own vendors. Section 2 (new Section 9(vv)) lists the diligence factors agencies must assess (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm). DOE confirms the April 13, 2026 signing, extension through FY2031, new security due-diligence mandates, and the reopened Phase II money (https://www.energy.gov/technologycommercialization/doe-small-business-innovation-research-sbir-and-small-business). The hard part is not screening names but LP-level look-through on venture funds, which is opaque and which no compliance vendor packages for a 4-person startup. Caveat: I could not confirm which agencies have opened T&BA vendor lists yet, so check that first.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a free 'SBIR foreign-risk self-check' web tool on top of the BIS Consolidated Screening List API and the UFLPA list. Use it as the lead magnet. Weeks 1 to 2: pull the last 12 months of Phase I/II awardees from the public SBIR.gov awards data and email 300 founders quoting the exact statute language. Weeks 2 to 4: manually produce 5 free dossiers for design partners to learn where the LP look-through breaks. Ask each agency SBIR office (start with DOE OTC, NSF and Navy) how to be listed as a T&BA vendor. Close 5 paid packs at $2.5k to $6.5k.

title: Public-Records Vault for City Employee AI Chats
one_liner: Capture, retain, redact and produce every government employee's AI prompt and response as the public record it legally is.
customer: City clerks, county records officers and city attorneys at cities of 20-300K people that just rolled out AI assistants to staff.
problem: Every prompt and output from a government employee is likely a public record subject to retention schedules and open-records requests. Cities are turning AI on in Chattanooga-style rollouts with no retention system. A single request from a journalist could force manual digging through vendor logs the city may not control.
solution: Browser extension and API proxy that captures AI interactions across tools, tags them to retention schedules, redacts exempt content (personnel, law enforcement, attorney-client), and generates one-click productions for open-records requests. Litigation-hold support included.
why_now: Local AI adoption is now real, with police, school and bus-routing deployments. GenAI.mil users have built more than 100k agents. Records lawyers are starting to warn, and the first open-records fights over chatbot logs will land in 2026-27.
revenue_model: $8-40K per year per city by headcount, plus e-discovery production fees. Reseller channel via records-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: AI adoption creates a records problem before it creates a safety problem. The clerk, not the CIO, has a legal deadline and a small budget line for exactly this.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 city clerks and 3 state records associations. Build the capture extension for two chat tools and a retention-schedule mapper. Pilot free with 2 cities that have announced AI programs, and convert on the first open-records request.
